sets.title: Smoothies and fruit salad
sets.contentHtml:
Ganga, Kaveri, and Narmada are three women who buy four raw materials (Mango, Apple, Banana and Milk) and sell five finished products (Mango smoothie, Apple smoothie, Banana smoothie, Mixed fruit smoothie and Fruit salad). Table-1 gives information about the raw materials required to produce the five finished products. One unit of a finished product requires one unit of each of the raw materials mentioned in the second column of the table.

Table I
Finished productRaw materials required
Mango smoothieMango, Milk
Apple smoothieApple, Milk
Banana smoothieBanana, Milk
Mixed fruit smoothieMango, Apple, Banana, Milk
Fruit saladMango, Apple, Banana

One unit of milk, mango, apple, and banana cost ₹5, ₹3, ₹2, and ₹1 respectively. Each unit of a finished product is sold for a profit equal to two times the number of raw materials used to make that product. For example, apple smoothie is made with two raw materials (apple and milk) and will be sold for a profit of ₹4 per unit. Leftover raw materials are sold during the last business hour of the day for a loss of ₹1 per unit.

The amount, in rupees, received from sales (revenue) for each woman in each of the four business hours of the day is given in Table-2.

Table II
Business HourGangaKaveriNarmada
Hour 1231931
Hour 2212221
Hour 3293023
Hour 4 (last hour)302722

The following additional facts are known.

  1. No one except possibly Ganga sold any Mango smoothie.
  2. Each woman sold either zero or one unit of any single finished product in any hour.
  3. Each woman had exactly one unit each of two different raw materials as leftovers.
  4. No one had any banana leftover.

sets.title: Journal papers by eight authors
sets.contentHtml:
A journal plans to publish 18 research papers, written by eight authors (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H) in four issues of the journal scheduled in January, April, July and October. Each of the research papers was written by exactly one of the eight authors. Five papers were scheduled in each of the first two issues, while four were scheduled in each of the last two issues. Every author wrote at least one paper and at most three papers. The total number of papers written by A, D, G and H was double the total number of papers written by the other four authors.

Four of the authors were from India and two each were from Japan and China. Each author belonged to exactly one of the three areas — Manufacturing, Automation and Logistics. Four of the authors were from the Logistics area and two were from the Automation area. As per the journal policy, none of the authors could have more than one paper in any issue of the journal.

The following facts are also known.

  1. F, an Indian author from the Logistics area, wrote only one paper. It was scheduled in the October issue.
  2. A was from the Automation area and did not have a paper scheduled in the October issue.
  3. None of the Indian authors were from the Manufacturing area and none of the Japanese or Chinese authors were from the Automation area.
  4. A and H were from different countries, but had their papers scheduled in exactly the same issues.
  5. C and E, both Chinese authors from different areas, had the same number of papers scheduled. Further, E had papers scheduled in consecutive issues of the journal but C did not.
  6. B, from the Logistics area, had a paper scheduled in the April issue of the journal.
  7. B and G belonged to the same country. None of their papers were scheduled in the same issue of the journal.
  8. D, a Japanese author from the Manufacturing area, did not have a paper scheduled in the July issue.
  9. C and H belonged to different areas.

sets.title: Friends, acquaintances and strangers
sets.contentHtml:
Amudha, Bharatan, Chandran, Dhinesh, Ezhil, Fani and Gowtham are seven people in a town. Any pair of them could either be strangers, acquaintances, or friends. All relationships are mutual. For example, if Amudha is a friend of Bharatan, then Bharatan is also a friend of Amudha. Similarly, if Amudha is a stranger to Bharatan, then Bharatan is also a stranger to Amudha.

Partial information about the number of friends, acquaintances, and strangers of each of these people among them is given in the table below.

No. of FriendsNo. of AcquaintancesNo. of Strangers
Amudha14
Bharatan
Chandran1
Dhinesh2
Ezhil1
Fani1
Gowtham32

The following additional facts are also known.

  1. Amudha, Bharatan, and Chandran are mutual strangers.
  2. Amudha, Dhinesh, and Fani are Ezhil's friends.
  3. Chandran and Gowtham are friends.
  4. Every friend of Amudha is an acquaintance of Bharatan, and every acquaintance of Bharatan is a friend of Amudha.
  5. Every friend of Bharatan is an acquaintance of Amudha, and every acquaintance of Amudha is a friend of Bharatan.

questions.solutionHtml:
Reading the chart (₹ million, 2019 → 2020, approx.): Furniture: Bookcases 1.9 → 2.2, Chairs 6.1 → 7.0, Furnishings 2.0 → 2.1, Tables 4.4 → 4.5. Office supply: Binders 3.6 → 5.3, Art 0.45 → 0.6, Appliances 1.9 → 3.1, Envelopes 0.35 → 0.2, Fasteners 0.1 → 0.1, Labels 0.2 → 0.3, Paper 1.5 → 2.0, Storage 4.3 → 5.1, Supplies 1.05 → 1.2. Technology: Accessories 3.05 → 4.4, Copiers 3.65 → 4.6, Machines 4.1 → 3.2, Phones 5.8 → 7.7.

Add the 2019 ticks of the nine office-supply subcategories: 3.6 + 0.45 + 1.9 + 0.35 + 0.1 + 0.2 + 1.5 + 4.3 + 1.05 ≈ 13.5.

questions.stemHtml: What BEST can be concluded about the number of units of fruit salad sold in the first hour?
questions.solutionHtml:
Prices. Price = cost + 2 × (number of raw materials): Mango smoothie 8 + 4 = 12, Apple smoothie 7 + 4 = 11, Banana smoothie 6 + 4 = 10, Mixed fruit smoothie 11 + 8 = 19, Fruit salad 6 + 6 = 12. Leftovers sell at cost − 1: mango 2, apple 1, milk 4 (no banana leftovers). Two different leftovers give mango+apple = 3, mango+milk = 6 or apple+milk = 5, all sold in hour 4.

Decoding the hours (each product at most once per hour, Mango smoothie only for Ganga):

  • Kaveri: 19 = Mixed; 22 = Banana + Salad; 30 = Apple + Mixed; hour 4: 27 − 6 = 21 = Apple + Banana (leftover mango+milk) or 27 − 5 = 22 = Banana + Salad (leftover apple+milk). 27 − 3 = 24 is impossible for her.
  • Narmada: 31 = Salad + Mixed; 21 = Apple + Banana; 23 = Apple + Salad; hour 4: only 22 − 3 = 19 = Mixed works, so her leftovers are mango+apple.
  • Ganga: 23 = Apple + Salad or Apple + Mango smoothie; 21 = Apple + Banana; 29 = Banana + Mixed; hour 4: only 30 − 6 = 24 = Mango smoothie + Salad works, so her leftovers are mango+milk.

Hour 1: Kaveri sold only a Mixed smoothie (0 salads), Narmada sold Salad + Mixed (1 salad), and Ganga’s 23 is Apple + Salad or Apple + Mango smoothie (1 or 0 salads).

Total fruit salads in hour 1 = either 1 or 2.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is NECESSARILY true?

options.textHtml: Narmada sold one unit of leftover milk.
Ganga did not sell any leftover mangoes.
Ganga did not sell any leftover apples.
Kaveri sold one unit of leftover mangoes

questions.solutionHtml:
Prices. Price = cost + 2 × (number of raw materials): Mango smoothie 8 + 4 = 12, Apple smoothie 7 + 4 = 11, Banana smoothie 6 + 4 = 10, Mixed fruit smoothie 11 + 8 = 19, Fruit salad 6 + 6 = 12. Leftovers sell at cost − 1: mango 2, apple 1, milk 4 (no banana leftovers). Two different leftovers give mango+apple = 3, mango+milk = 6 or apple+milk = 5, all sold in hour 4.

Decoding the hours (each product at most once per hour, Mango smoothie only for Ganga):

  • Kaveri: 19 = Mixed; 22 = Banana + Salad; 30 = Apple + Mixed; hour 4: 27 − 6 = 21 = Apple + Banana (leftover mango+milk) or 27 − 5 = 22 = Banana + Salad (leftover apple+milk). 27 − 3 = 24 is impossible for her.
  • Narmada: 31 = Salad + Mixed; 21 = Apple + Banana; 23 = Apple + Salad; hour 4: only 22 − 3 = 19 = Mixed works, so her leftovers are mango+apple.
  • Ganga: 23 = Apple + Salad or Apple + Mango smoothie; 21 = Apple + Banana; 29 = Banana + Mixed; hour 4: only 30 − 6 = 24 = Mango smoothie + Salad works, so her leftovers are mango+milk.

Ganga’s hour-4 revenue of 30 works only with leftovers mango + milk (6) plus Mango smoothie + Salad (24). So she had no leftover apple, and C is necessarily true.

A is false (Narmada’s leftovers are mango + apple). B is false (Ganga did sell a leftover mango). D is only possible: Kaveri may have had apple + milk instead.

questions.stemHtml: What BEST can be concluded about the total number of units of milk the three women had in the beginning?
questions.solutionHtml:
Prices. Price = cost + 2 × (number of raw materials): Mango smoothie 8 + 4 = 12, Apple smoothie 7 + 4 = 11, Banana smoothie 6 + 4 = 10, Mixed fruit smoothie 11 + 8 = 19, Fruit salad 6 + 6 = 12. Leftovers sell at cost − 1: mango 2, apple 1, milk 4 (no banana leftovers). Two different leftovers give mango+apple = 3, mango+milk = 6 or apple+milk = 5, all sold in hour 4.

Decoding the hours (each product at most once per hour, Mango smoothie only for Ganga):

  • Kaveri: 19 = Mixed; 22 = Banana + Salad; 30 = Apple + Mixed; hour 4: 27 − 6 = 21 = Apple + Banana (leftover mango+milk) or 27 − 5 = 22 = Banana + Salad (leftover apple+milk). 27 − 3 = 24 is impossible for her.
  • Narmada: 31 = Salad + Mixed; 21 = Apple + Banana; 23 = Apple + Salad; hour 4: only 22 − 3 = 19 = Mixed works, so her leftovers are mango+apple.
  • Ganga: 23 = Apple + Salad or Apple + Mango smoothie; 21 = Apple + Banana; 29 = Banana + Mixed; hour 4: only 30 − 6 = 24 = Mango smoothie + Salad works, so her leftovers are mango+milk.

Milk goes into every smoothie (not the salad), plus any leftover milk.

Ganga: hour 1 Apple + (Salad or Mango smoothie) = 1 or 2; hour 2 = 2; hour 3 = 2; hour 4 Mango smoothie = 1; leftover milk 1. Total 7 or 8.

Kaveri: hour 1 = 1; hour 2 = 1; hour 3 = 2; hour 4 is either Apple + Banana (2) + leftover milk (1) = 3, or Banana + Salad (1) + leftover milk (1) = 2. Total 6 or 7.

Narmada: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5, no leftover milk.

Total = 18, 19 or 20, and all three are achievable, so the answer is D.

questions.stemHtml: If it is known that three leftover units of mangoes were sold during the last business hour of the day, how many apple smoothies were sold during the day?
questions.solutionHtml:
Prices. Price = cost + 2 × (number of raw materials): Mango smoothie 8 + 4 = 12, Apple smoothie 7 + 4 = 11, Banana smoothie 6 + 4 = 10, Mixed fruit smoothie 11 + 8 = 19, Fruit salad 6 + 6 = 12. Leftovers sell at cost − 1: mango 2, apple 1, milk 4 (no banana leftovers). Two different leftovers give mango+apple = 3, mango+milk = 6 or apple+milk = 5, all sold in hour 4.

Decoding the hours (each product at most once per hour, Mango smoothie only for Ganga):

  • Kaveri: 19 = Mixed; 22 = Banana + Salad; 30 = Apple + Mixed; hour 4: 27 − 6 = 21 = Apple + Banana (leftover mango+milk) or 27 − 5 = 22 = Banana + Salad (leftover apple+milk). 27 − 3 = 24 is impossible for her.
  • Narmada: 31 = Salad + Mixed; 21 = Apple + Banana; 23 = Apple + Salad; hour 4: only 22 − 3 = 19 = Mixed works, so her leftovers are mango+apple.
  • Ganga: 23 = Apple + Salad or Apple + Mango smoothie; 21 = Apple + Banana; 29 = Banana + Mixed; hour 4: only 30 − 6 = 24 = Mango smoothie + Salad works, so her leftovers are mango+milk.

Ganga and Narmada already have a leftover mango each, so the third must be Kaveri’s. Her leftovers are mango + milk, and her hour-4 sales are Apple + Banana.

Apple smoothies: Ganga 2 (hours 1 and 2, since both hour-1 options include an apple smoothie), Kaveri 2 (hours 3 and 4), Narmada 2 (hours 2 and 3).

Total = 6.

questions.stemHtml: What is the correct sequence of number of papers written by B, C, E and G, respectively?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. A + D + G + H = 12 with at most 3 each, so each of A, D, G, H wrote 3; B + C + E + F = 6 with F = 1 and C = E.

Automation authors must be Indian (fact 3), so A is Indian and H (different country) is not. C, E are the Chinese, so H and D are Japanese; B and G (same country) are then Indian, with F and A. C and E are in different areas, neither Automation, so one is Manufacturing and one is Logistics. With D, that fills Manufacturing, so H is Logistics, C is Manufacturing (fact 9) and E is Logistics. Logistics = F, B, H, E, so the second Automation author is G.

Issues: A and H: Jan, Apr, Jul. D: Jan, Apr, Oct. G avoids B’s April, so G: Jan, Jul, Oct, and B can then only be in April, so B = 1 and C = E = 2. One slot is left in each issue; E takes consecutive issues and C does not, so C: Jan, Oct and E: Apr, Jul.

IssuePapers (author: country, area)
Jan (5)A (Ind, Aut), H (Jap, Log), D (Jap, Man), G (Ind, Aut), C (Chi, Man)
Apr (5)A (Ind, Aut), H (Jap, Log), D (Jap, Man), B (Ind, Log), E (Chi, Log)
Jul (4)A (Ind, Aut), H (Jap, Log), G (Ind, Aut), E (Chi, Log)
Oct (4)D (Jap, Man), G (Ind, Aut), F (Ind, Log), C (Chi, Man)

B = 1, C = 2, E = 2, G = 3, which is option C.

questions.stemHtml: Who are Gowtham’s acquaintances?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions (each person has 6 relationships).
